title: Δῶρα μνηστήρων
about: Penelope's rebuke of Telemachus for letting the stranger be struck gives the part its opening, and he answers her: he knows right from wrong, but the suitors crowd him and he has no helpers, and he wishes them all as limp as Irus now sits at the gate. Eurymachus flatters Penelope, saying more suitors would feast in her house if all the Achaeans could see her; she answers that the gods destroyed her beauty when Odysseus sailed, and she quotes his parting words to her, to marry when their son has a beard. Antinous tells her to accept the gifts, and each suitor sends a herald to fetch one; Penelope goes up to her rooms with the gifts. The suitors dance and sing until evening, braziers are set up, and Odysseus, in disguise, sends the maids to Penelope and takes over the lighting himself, saying that he will outlast them all until dawn.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχ’, οὐκέτι τοι φρένες ἔμπεδοι οὐδὲ νόημα·
sentences.l: “Telemachus, no longer are your wits firm, nor your thought;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, your wits are no longer firm, nor is your thinking;
sentences.n: Penelope's speech, which the introduction at 18.214 (the last unit of the previous part) has just announced, begins here. Τηλέμαχ’ is the vocative with its final vowel elided. οὐκέτι τοι: τοι is the dative of σύ, 'to you', used as an appeal to the listener ('you see'). φρένες 'wits' and νόημα 'thought' are two subjects of one understood 'are', and ἔμπεδοι 'firm, steady' agrees with the nearer one, φρένες. The line is a flat reproach, the first of two built on the same words (220 repeats it).

sentences.t: παῖς ἔτ’ ἐὼν καὶ μᾶλλον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ κέρδε’ ἐνώμας·
sentences.l: a child still being, and more, in your mind cunning-ways you used to turn over;
sentences.i: even when you were still a child you turned cunning ways over in your mind, and more than now;
sentences.n: ἐών is the epic participle of εἰμί (Attic ὤν), and παῖς ἔτ’ ἐών 'though still a child' sets the past against νῦν in the next line. κέρδε’ is the uncontracted plural κέρδεα, elided: κέρδος is 'gain', and in the plural 'cunning ways, clever schemes' (the house rendering of κέρδεα), a word that praises cleverness without yet judging it. ἐνώμας is the imperfect of ἐνωμάω 'handle, turn over', a repeated action in the past: 'you used to'. καὶ μᾶλλον 'and more' is left without its second half, which νῦν supplies.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’, ὅτε δὴ μέγας ἐσσὶ καὶ ἥβης μέτρον ἱκάνεις,
καί κέν τις φαίη γόνον ἔμμεναι ὀλβίου ἀνδρός,
ἐς μέγεθος καὶ κάλλος ὁρώμενος, ἀλλότριος φώς,
οὐκέτι τοι φρένες εἰσὶν ἐναίσιμοι οὐδὲ νόημα.
sentences.l:
but now, when you are great and are reaching the measure of youth,
and even someone might say you are the offspring of a prosperous man,
looking to your stature and beauty, a foreign man,
no longer are your wits fitting, nor your thought.
sentences.i: but now that you are big and are coming to the measure of youth, so that even a foreign man, looking at your stature and beauty, might say you were the son of a prosperous man, your wits are no longer fitting, nor your thinking;
sentences.n: One sentence, four lines long: the clause νῦν δ’ ὅτε … ἱκάνεις gives the time, καί κέν τις φαίη … ἀλλότριος φώς says what a stranger might think, and the main statement is the last line, which repeats line 215 with ἐναίσιμοι 'fitting' for ἔμπεδοι 'firm': the same charge, put once more. ἐσσί is the epic second person of εἰμί (Attic εἶ), and ἥβης μέτρον ἱκάνεις is 'you are reaching the measure of youth'. φαίη is the optative of φημί, with κέν (= ἄν) making it 'might say', and γόνον ἔμμεναι ὀλβίου ἀνδρός is 'that you are the offspring of a prosperous man' (ἔμμεναι, epic for εἶναι). ὁρώμενος is a middle participle of ὁράω, agreeing with τις: 'looking at you'. ἀλλότριος φώς is 'a foreign man', φώς being 'man'.

sentences.t:
οἷον δὴ τόδε ἔργον ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἐτύχθη,
ὃς τὸν ξεῖνον ἔασας ἀεικισθήμεναι οὕτως.
sentences.l:
What a deed this was, in the halls it was done,
you who the stranger allowed to be treated unseemly so!
sentences.i: What a deed this is, that has been done in these halls, you who let the stranger be treated in so unseemly a way!
sentences.n: οἷον with rough breathing is the exclamatory 'what a thing'; with smooth breathing, οἶον, it is 'alone', and the two need telling apart. ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω 'make', so 'was brought about, was done'. ὅς here is a relative that picks up the 'you' of the vocative: 'you who', ὅς with the second person understood. ἔασας is the aorist of ἐάω 'allow', and ἀεικισθήμεναι the aorist passive infinitive of ἀεικίζω 'treat unseemly, mistreat', with the old ending -μεναι (Attic -θῆναι); ἀεικής 'unseemly' is its adjective. τὸν ξεῖνον is 'the stranger', the pronoun τόν used close to an article, and the stranger is Odysseus the beggar.

sentences.t:
πῶς νῦν, εἴ τι ξεῖνος ἐν ἡμετέροισι δόμοισιν
ἥμενος ὧδε πάθοι ῥυστακτύος ἐξ ἀλεγεινῆς;
sentences.l:
How now, if some stranger in our house,
sitting thus, were to suffer anything from grievous rough-handling?
sentences.i: What then, if a stranger sitting here like this in our house were to suffer anything from such grievous rough handling?
sentences.n: A question, ending in the Greek question mark. πῶς νῦν 'how then' is rhetorical. εἴ τι ... πάθοι is a remote condition: εἰ with the aorist optative of πάσχω 'suffer'; its result follows in the next line, with κε and the optative. ἡμετέροισι δόμοισιν is the dative plural in -οισι(ν), 'in our house', the plural δόμοι standing for one dwelling. ἥμενος ὧδε is 'sitting just so', as the stranger sits now. ῥυστακτύς occurs only here in Homer; it is built on the root of ῥυστάζω 'pull about, haul', and 'rough handling, being dragged about' is what the root suggests, not a meaning known from other uses. ἀλεγεινῆς is 'grievous'.

sentences.t: σοί κ’ αἶσχος λώβη τε μετ’ ἀνθρώποισι πέλοιτο.
sentences.l: to you disgrace and outrage among men would come.”
sentences.i: Disgrace and outrage would fall upon you among men.”
sentences.n: The result clause of the condition begun in the line before: σοί 'to you' comes first, for emphasis, and κ’ is κε (= ἄν) with the optative πέλοιτο, 'would come to be', πέλω being an epic verb for 'be, come to be'. αἶσχος is 'disgrace' and λώβη 'outrage', shameful abuse of a person; both are nominative subjects, and μετ’ ἀνθρώποισι is 'among men' with the dative in -οισι. This ends Penelope's first speech, and the closing quotation mark is ours: Murray prints none.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction. τὴν δ’ αὖ is 'to her in turn', τήν a pronoun, and ηὔδα the unaugmented imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'. ἀντίον is the adverb 'face to face, directly'. πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is the standing epithet of Telemachus, translated every time even where it sits oddly: here he is about to answer a rebuke for want of sense.

sentences.t: μῆτερ ἐμή, τὸ μὲν οὔ σε νεμεσσῶμαι κεχολῶσθαι·
sentences.l: “Mother mine, in this at least I do not resent you for being angry;
sentences.i: “Mother, I do not blame you for being angry at this;
sentences.n: Telemachus' reply. μῆτερ ἐμή is 'my mother', the vocative with the possessive after it. τὸ μέν is an accusative of respect, 'in this, at least', and νεμεσσῶμαι is the contracted first person of νεμεσσάομαι 'feel righteous resentment at', here with a person (σε) and an infinitive. κεχολῶσθαι is the perfect infinitive of χολόω 'be angry': 'that you have become angry, are angry'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ θυμῷ νοέω καὶ οἶδα ἕκαστα,
ἐσθλά τε καὶ τὰ χέρεια·
sentences.l:
but I in my heart perceive and know each thing,
the good and the worse;
sentences.i: but in my heart I perceive and know each thing, both the good and the worse;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is the epic 'but, and yet'. θυμῷ is the dative 'in my heart', νοέω 'perceive, understand', and οἶδα 'I know'; ἕκαστα is 'each thing, everything one by one'. ἐσθλά 'good things' and τὰ χέρεια 'the worse' are in apposition to ἕκαστα. χέρεια is the neuter plural of χερείων, an old comparative of κακός 'bad'. The raised point ends the unit in the middle of line 229.

sentences.t: πάρος δ’ ἔτι νήπιος ἦα.
sentences.l: before, I was still foolish.
sentences.i: before now I was still foolish.
sentences.n: πάρος 'formerly, before' and ἦα, the epic imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). νήπιος is literally 'not speaking', an infant, and then 'foolish, blind to what is coming'; the house rendering is 'foolish', but here a grown man looks back on his childhood, and the sense 'childish, immature' lies under it. The raised point stands in the middle of line 229, so this unit is the second half of the line.

sentences.t: ἀλλά τοι οὐ δύναμαι πεπνυμένα πάντα νοῆσαι·
sentences.l: But, I tell you, I am not able all prudent things to think of;
sentences.i: but I am not able to think of everything that would be prudent;
sentences.n: τοι is again 'I tell you'. πεπνυμένα is the neuter plural of Telemachus' own epithet, and is best taken as 'prudent things': πάντα πεπνυμένα νοῆσαι 'to think out all prudent things'; some take it adverbially, 'to think everything out prudently', and the sense is close. νοῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of νοέω, the verb of line 228.

sentences.t:
ἐκ γάρ με πλήσσουσι παρήμενοι ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος
οἵδε κακὰ φρονέοντες, ἐμοὶ δ’ οὐκ εἰσὶν ἀρωγοί.
sentences.l:
for they strike me out of my wits, sitting beside me, one from one side, another from another,
these men, thinking evil, and to me there are no helpers.
sentences.i: For these men sit around me and strike me out of my senses, one from one side and one from another, meaning evil, and I have no helpers.
sentences.n: ἐκ ... πλήσσουσι is tmesis: the preverb stands apart from its verb, and together they are ἐκπλήσσουσι 'strike out of one's wits, daunt'. παρήμενοι is 'sitting beside', and ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος 'one from one side, another from another'. οἵδε is 'these men here', the suitors, who are present as he speaks. κακὰ φρονέοντες is 'thinking evil', φρονέοντες the uncontracted participle (Attic φρονοῦντες). ἐμοὶ δ’ οὐκ εἰσὶν ἀρωγοί is 'and to me there are no helpers'; ἀρωγός is 'one who comes to help'.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν τοι ξείνου γε καὶ Ἴρου μῶλος ἐτύχθη
μνηστήρων ἰότητι, βίῃ δ’ ὅ γε φέρτερος ἦεν.
sentences.l:
Not indeed of the stranger and Irus the struggle came about
by the suitors' will, but in strength he was the stronger.
sentences.i: The struggle between the stranger and Irus did not come about by the suitors' will; the stranger was the stronger in force.
sentences.n: οὐ μέν τοι is 'indeed not'. μῶλος is 'toil of battle, struggle', a word of war used here for a fight between two beggars. ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω 'make, bring about', as in line 221. ἰότητι is a dative of ἰότης 'will, favour' (the house word is 'will'): 'by the will of'. ὅ γε is 'he', and picks out the stranger, the winner; βίῃ is a dative of respect 'in strength, in force'; φέρτερος is the comparative 'stronger, better'; ἦεν is the epic ἦν.

sentences.t:
αἲ γάρ, Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον,
οὕτω νῦν μνηστῆρες ἐν ἡμετέροισι δόμοισι
νεύοιεν κεφαλὰς δεδμημένοι, οἱ μὲν ἐν αὐλῇ,
οἱ δ’ ἔντοσθε δόμοιο, λελῦτο δὲ γυῖα ἑκάστου,
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
thus now the suitors in our house
might nod their heads, overpowered, some in the courtyard,
others inside the house, and loosened be the limbs of each one,
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — the suitors in our house might now nod their heads, overpowered, some in the courtyard and some inside the house, with the limbs of every one of them loosened,
sentences.n: A wish, and the first line of it stands word for word in an earlier part (4.341). αἲ γάρ introduces a wish (= εἰ γάρ), and the verb is the optative νεύοιεν, 'might nod'. δεδμημένοι is the perfect passive participle of δάμνημι 'overpower, subdue'. οἱ μέν ... οἱ δέ are 'some ... others', and ἔντοσθε is 'inside', with the genitive. λελῦτο is usually taken as a perfect optative of λύω 'loosen', so the wish runs on: 'and may the limbs of each be loosened'. The wish is completed by ὡς, 'just as', in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὡς νῦν Ἶρος κεῖνος ἐπ’ αὐλείῃσι θύρῃσιν
ἧσται νευστάζων κεφαλῇ, μεθύοντι ἐοικώς,
οὐδ’ ὀρθὸς στῆναι δύναται ποσὶν οὐδὲ νέεσθαι
οἴκαδ’, ὅπη οἱ νόστος, ἐπεὶ φίλα γυῖα λέλυνται.
sentences.l:
just as now Irus that one, at the courtyard doors,
sits, nodding with his head, like one drunk,
and cannot stand upright on his feet, nor go
home, where his homecoming lies, since his dear limbs are loosened.”
sentences.i: just as Irus there now sits at the courtyard doors, nodding his head like a drunken man, and cannot stand upright on his feet or go back home, wherever his homecoming lies, since his dear limbs are loosened.”
sentences.n: ὡς νῦν 'just as now' answers the wish of the unit before. Ἶρος κεῖνος is 'that Irus', κεῖνος the epic form of ἐκεῖνος, and ἐπ’ αὐλείῃσι θύρῃσιν is 'at the courtyard doors', the dative in -ῃσι. ἧσται is the perfect middle of ἧμαι 'sit'. νευστάζων 'nodding' is a repeated form of νεύω, the verb of line 237, and μεθύοντι ἐοικώς is 'like one who is drunk' (ἐοικώς, perfect participle, with the dative). νέεσθαι is the epic infinitive 'to go'. ὅπη οἱ νόστος is 'where for him is the way home', with νόστος 'homecoming'. λέλυνται is the perfect passive of λύω, the plain form of λελῦτο above; φίλα here is 'his own dear'. Telemachus' speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον·
sentences.l: So they, such things to one another were saying;
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another;
sentences.n: ὣς οἱ μὲν is 'so they', that is Penelope and Telemachus, and δέ in the next line brings in the new speaker. τοιαῦτα is 'such things', πρὸς ἀλλήλους 'to one another', and ἀγόρευον the imperfect of ἀγορεύω 'speak'. The line stands in an earlier part with a comma and a further line; here it stands alone before the raised point.

sentences.t: Εὐρύμαχος δ’ ἐπέεσσι προσηύδα Πηνελόπειαν·
sentences.l: and Eurymachus with words spoke to Penelope:
sentences.i: and Eurymachus spoke to Penelope:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction. ἐπέεσσι is the uncontracted dative plural of ἔπος (Attic ἔπεσι), 'with words'; προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω 'speak to', and Πηνελόπειαν is the accusative of the person addressed.

sentences.t:
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρον Πηνελόπεια,
εἰ πάντες σε ἴδοιεν ἀν’ Ἴασον Ἄργος Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.l:
“Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope,
if all the Achaeans were to see you throughout Iasian Argos,
sentences.i: “Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, if all the Achaeans were to see you throughout Iasian Argos,
sentences.n: The vocative κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο is 'daughter of Icarius', with the genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου); περίφρον is 'circumspect', the standing epithet of Penelope, here in the vocative. εἰ ... ἴδοιεν is a remote condition with the aorist optative, and its result begins in the next line. ἀν’ is ἀνά 'up and down, throughout', with the accusative. Ἴασον Ἄργος 'Iasian Argos' is a name whose exact reach is not known: Argos here is a wide region, probably the Peloponnese or Greece in general, and the meaning of Ἴασον is not certain. The cut is made after the condition, where the syntax pauses, because the whole sentence runs to five lines.

sentences.t:
πλέονές κε μνηστῆρες ἐν ὑμετέροισι δόμοισιν
ἠῶθεν δαινύατ’, ἐπεὶ περίεσσι γυναικῶν
εἶδός τε μέγεθός τε ἰδὲ φρένας ἔνδον ἐΐσας.
sentences.l:
more suitors in your house
at dawn would feast, since you surpass women
in looks and in stature and in the wits within, well-balanced.”
sentences.i: more suitors would be feasting in your house from dawn on, since you surpass all women in looks and stature, and in the well-balanced mind within.”
sentences.n: πλέονες is 'more', and ὑμετέροισι, 'your', is plural, as if for Penelope's household. ἠῶθεν is 'from dawn, in the morning'. δαινύατ’ is the optative δαινύατο (epic for δαινυίατο) of δαίνυμι 'feast', and κε makes it 'would'. περίεσσι is the second person of περίειμι 'surpass', with the genitive γυναικῶν. εἶδος is 'looks, form' and μέγεθος 'stature'. φρένας ἔνδον ἐΐσας is 'the wits within, well-balanced'; the line stands word for word in an earlier part (11.337); ἐΐσας is the feminine accusative plural of ἐΐσος, whose exact force here ('equal', 'balanced') is not certain, so this is only one way of taking it.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: Him then answered circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope answered him:
sentences.n: A reply-formula. τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is 'him then answered', ἠμείβετο being the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι 'reply'. περίφρων is the epithet of Penelope: 'circumspect', a compound of περί 'around, all round' and φρήν 'mind'.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύμαχ’, ἦ τοι ἐμὴν ἀρετὴν εἶδός τε δέμας τε
ὤλεσαν ἀθάνατοι, ὅτε Ἴλιον εἰσανέβαινον
Ἀργεῖοι, μετὰ τοῖσι δ’ ἐμὸς πόσις ᾖεν Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
“Eurymachus, truly my excellence, both form and body,
the immortals destroyed, when to Ilium they were going up,
the Argives, and among them my husband went, Odysseus.
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, the immortals destroyed my excellence, my form and my body, when the Argives went up to Ilium, and among them went my husband Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is 'truly, indeed'. ἀρετή is 'excellence', whatever makes a person admirable; Penelope names it as εἶδος 'form' and δέμας 'body', so that the two nouns after it say what her ἀρετή was, in answer to Eurymachus' εἶδος and μέγεθος. ὤλεσαν is the aorist of ὄλλυμι 'destroy', and ἀθάνατοι 'the immortals', the subject, comes after the verb. εἰσανέβαινον is the imperfect of εἰσαναβαίνω 'go up into': the Argives 'going up' to Ilium, the line not saying from where. Ἀργεῖοι 'Argives' is a name for the Greeks as a whole. μετὰ τοῖσι is 'among them' (τοῖσι a pronoun), and ᾖεν is the epic imperfect of εἶμι, 'went'.

sentences.t:
εἰ κεῖνός γ’ ἐλθὼν τὸν ἐμὸν βίον ἀμφιπολεύοι,
μεῖζόν κε κλέος εἴη ἐμὸν καὶ κάλλιον οὕτως.
sentences.l:
If he, having come, were to tend my life,
greater would my fame be and finer, thus.
sentences.i: If he came back and watched over my life, my fame would be greater and finer in that way.
sentences.n: A remote condition: εἰ with the optative ἀμφιπολεύοι, and κε with the optative εἴη in the result. ἀμφιπολεύω is 'attend to, look after', the verb that belongs to ἀμφίπολος 'attendant'. κεῖνός γε is 'that man, at least', and ἐλθών 'having come' means come home. βίον is 'life, living'. κλέος is 'fame', here a woman's reputation, and κάλλιον is 'finer, more beautiful', the comparative of καλός. οὕτως is 'thus, in that case'.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἄχομαι· τόσα γάρ μοι ἐπέσσευεν κακὰ δαίμων.
sentences.l: But now I grieve; for so many against me drove evils some power.
sentences.i: But now I grieve, for some power has driven so many evils upon me.
sentences.n: ἄχομαι is 'I am grieved', the verb that belongs to ἄχος 'grief', which returns in line 274. τόσα is 'so many', and μοι the dative 'against me, upon me'. ἐπέσσευεν is a past tense (the aorist) of ἐπισεύω 'drive on, hurl upon', with the doubled σ of its epic form. δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, 'some power': she does not say which god.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν δὴ ὅτε τ’ ᾖε λιπὼν κάτα πατρίδα γαῖαν,
δεξιτερὴν ἐπὶ καρπῷ ἑλὼν ἐμὲ χεῖρα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
Truly, when he went, leaving behind his fatherland,
his right hand at the wrist taking me, he spoke to me:
sentences.i: Indeed, when he went off, leaving his fatherland behind, he took me by the right hand at the wrist and spoke to me:
sentences.n: ἦ μὲν δή is 'truly, indeed', and ὅτε τ’ is 'when', with the epic τε. ᾖε is the imperfect of εἶμι (Attic ᾔει) 'went'. λιπὼν κάτα is 'leaving behind', the preverb κατά placed after its verb with the accent drawn back. πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'fatherland'. δεξιτερὴν ... χεῖρα is 'the right hand', and ἐπὶ καρπῷ 'at the wrist', καρπός being the wrist; ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, 'having taken', and ἐμέ 'me' with χεῖρα is the whole and the part: 'took me by the hand'. προσηύδα is 'spoke to', as in line 244. The raised point opens Odysseus' words, which Penelope now quotes.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι, οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιοὺς
ἐκ Τροίης εὖ πάντας ἀπήμονας ἀπονέεσθαι·
sentences.l:
‘Wife, for I do not think that the well-greaved Achaeans
from Troy, all well and unharmed, will return;
sentences.i: ‘Wife, I do not think that all the well-greaved Achaeans will come home from Troy well and unharmed;
sentences.n: Odysseus' words, as Penelope repeats them; the single quotation marks set them off inside her own speech. ὦ γύναι is 'wife', the address of a husband to a wife. ὀΐω is 'I think, suppose' (Attic οἴομαι), with an accusative and infinitive. ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς is the standing 'well-greaved Achaeans'. εὖ is 'well' and ἀπήμονας 'unharmed', said of persons, and both go with πάντας: 'all well, unharmed'. ἀπονέεσθαι is the epic present infinitive 'to go home', with the sense of a future.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ Τρῶάς φασι μαχητὰς ἔμμεναι ἄνδρας,
ἠμὲν ἀκοντιστὰς ἠδὲ ῥυτῆρας ὀϊστῶν
ἵππων τ’ ὠκυπόδων ἐπιβήτορας, οἵ κε τάχιστα
ἔκριναν μέγα νεῖκος ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο.
sentences.l:
for indeed the Trojans, they say, are fighting men,
both javelin-throwers and drawers of arrows
and mounters of swift-footed horses, who most quickly
decide the great strife of even-handed war.
sentences.i: for they say the Trojans too are fighting men, javelin-throwers and archers and riders of swift-footed horses, who are quickest to settle the great strife of even-handed war.
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is 'for indeed'. φασι is 'they say', with Τρῶας as subject of ἔμμεναι (the epic infinitive of εἰμί): 'they say the Trojans are fighting men'. ἀκοντιστάς are 'javelin-throwers', men who hurl the ἄκων 'javelin'. ῥυτῆρας ὀϊστῶν is literally 'drawers of arrows', that is, archers. ὠκυπόδων 'swift-footed' is a compound of ὠκύς 'swift' and πούς 'foot', and ἐπιβήτορας is 'mounters', riders. οἵ κε ... ἔκριναν is κε with the aorist indicative of κρίνω, a general statement: 'who are the ones to decide'. ὁμοιΐου is of uncertain force: 'impartial, common to both sides' is the usual gloss, and 'even-handed' is only one way of taking it.

sentences.t:
τῷ οὐκ οἶδ’ ἤ κέν μ’ ἀνέσει θεός, ἦ κεν ἁλώω
αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ·
sentences.l:
Therefore I do not know whether a god will let me go, or whether I shall be taken
on the spot in Troy;
sentences.i: so I do not know whether a god will let me go, or whether I shall be taken on the spot in Troy;
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore'. οὐκ οἶδ’ ἤ ... ἦ is 'I do not know whether ... or whether'. ἀνέσει is from ἀνίημι 'let go, release' (a future, or a short-vowel subjunctive with κε; the sense is the same: 'whether he will'). ἁλώω is the aorist subjunctive of ἁλίσκομαι 'be taken, captured', in the epic form with a lengthened vowel. αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ is 'on the spot, in Troy itself', with αὐτοῦ an adverb 'right there'. The raised point comes in the middle of line 266.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἐνθάδε πάντα μελόντων.
sentences.l: but for you here let all things be a care.
sentences.i: but let everything here be your care:
sentences.n: μελόντων is the third person plural imperative of μέλω 'be a care to', here with the dative σοί 'to you': 'let all things be a care to you'. ἐνθάδε is 'here', at home. The thought is completed by the infinitives of the next unit (μεμνῆσθαι), which stand as commands.

sentences.t:
μεμνῆσθαι πατρὸς καὶ μητέρος ἐν μεγάροισιν
ὡς νῦν, ἢ ἔτι μᾶλλον ἐμεῦ ἀπονόσφιν ἐόντος·
sentences.l:
to remember my father and mother in the halls
as now, or still more, while I am far away;
sentences.i: remember my father and my mother in the halls, as you do now, or even more, while I am far away;
sentences.n: μεμνῆσθαι is the perfect infinitive of μιμνῄσκομαι 'remember, be mindful of', with the genitive πατρός and μητέρος, an epic μητέρος (Attic μητρός). Like the infinitives that follow, it is used as an imperative: 'remember'. ἐν μεγάροισιν is 'in the halls', the dative in -οισι. ὡς νῦν ἢ ἔτι μᾶλλον is 'as now, or still more'. ἐμεῦ ... ἐόντος is a genitive absolute, 'I being', and ἀπονόσφιν 'far away, apart'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δὴ παῖδα γενειήσαντα ἴδηαι,
γήμασθ’ ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα, τεὸν κατὰ δῶμα λιποῦσα.
sentences.l:
but when indeed you see the boy bearded,
marry whom you wish, leaving your house behind.’
sentences.i: but when you see the boy grown a beard, marry whomever you wish, and leave your house behind.’
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν is 'but when', with the subjunctive ἴδηαι, the epic second person of the aorist subjunctive of ὁράω, 'you see'. γενειήσαντα is the aorist participle of γενειάω 'grow a beard', here of Telemachus, whom Odysseus calls simply παῖδα 'the boy'. γήμασθ’ is the aorist middle infinitive γήμασθαι 'to marry' used as an imperative, and ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is 'whom you wish', ἐθέλῃσθα being the epic ending of the second person. τεὸν is the epic form of σόν 'your'. κατὰ ... λιποῦσα is tmesis, καταλιποῦσα 'leaving behind'. This is the end of Odysseus' words as Penelope quotes them, and the single closing quotation mark is ours.

sentences.t: κεῖνος τὼς ἀγόρευε·
sentences.l: That man thus was speaking;
sentences.i: That is how he spoke;
sentences.n: Penelope is speaking again in her own voice. κεῖνος is 'that man', Odysseus, and τὼς is the epic adverb 'thus' (Attic οὕτως). ἀγόρευε is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω 'speak'.

sentences.t: τὰ δὴ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται.
sentences.l: these things now all are being fulfilled.
sentences.i: and now all of it is being fulfilled.
sentences.n: τὰ δή is 'these things indeed'. τελεῖται is a present passive, 'is being accomplished, is being brought to an end', of τελέω; it can also be read as a future, and the sense 'is coming true' covers both.

sentences.t:
νὺξ δ’ ἔσται ὅτε δὴ στυγερὸς γάμος ἀντιβολήσει
οὐλομένης ἐμέθεν, τῆς τε Ζεὺς ὄλβον ἀπηύρα.
sentences.l:
And night will be when the hateful marriage will meet
me, the ruined, of whom Zeus took away prosperity.
sentences.i: A night is coming when the hateful marriage will meet me, ruined as I am, from whom Zeus has taken away prosperity.
sentences.n: νὺξ δ’ ἔσται ὅτε δή is 'and there will be a night when'. στυγερός is 'hateful', and the marriage is the one she is to be forced into. ἀντιβολήσει is the future of ἀντιβολέω 'meet, encounter', with the genitive οὐλομένης ἐμέθεν; ἐμέθεν is an epic genitive of ἐγώ, and οὐλομένης 'ruined, accursed' is a participle of ὄλλυμι, meaning 'the doomed one'. τῆς τε is a relative with the epic τε: 'of whom'. ἀπηύρα is the aorist of ἀπαυράω 'take away', with ὄλβον as its object and τῆς, in the genitive, the person deprived. ὄλβον is 'prosperity'.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τόδ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἱκάνει·
sentences.l: But this fearsome grief reaches my heart and spirit;
sentences.i: But this fearsome grief comes upon my heart and spirit;
sentences.n: αἰνὸν ἄχος is 'fearsome grief'; ἄχος belongs with ἄχομαι of line 256, and αἰνός is the house 'fearsome'. κραδίην καὶ θυμόν is 'heart and spirit', two words kept apart when they stand together. ἱκάνει is 'reaches, comes to', from the same verb as line 217. The grief that follows is not the marriage itself but the way the suitors behave.

sentences.t: μνηστήρων οὐχ ἥδε δίκη τὸ πάροιθε τέτυκτο·
sentences.l: of suitors not this the custom in former times was set;
sentences.i: this was not the custom of suitors in former times;
sentences.n: μνηστήρων is the genitive 'of suitors', and δίκη here is 'custom, way of acting', not 'justice'. τὸ πάροιθε is 'formerly, before', τό being an adverbial accusative. τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω 'had been made, had been established'.

sentences.t:
οἵ τ’ ἀγαθήν τε γυναῖκα καὶ ἀφνειοῖο θύγατρα
μνηστεύειν ἐθέλωσι καὶ ἀλλήλοις ἐρίσωσιν,
αὐτοὶ τοί γ’ ἀπάγουσι βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα,
κούρης δαῖτα φίλοισι, καὶ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα διδοῦσιν·
sentences.l:
who a good woman and a rich man's daughter
wish to woo, and with one another contend,
they themselves bring cattle and stout flocks,
for the girl a feast for her dear ones, and give splendid gifts;
sentences.i: Men who wish to woo a good woman, the daughter of a rich man, and who contend with one another, bring cattle and stout flocks themselves, a feast for the girl's own people, and give splendid gifts;
sentences.n: The sentence is a general statement: οἵ τε ... ἐθέλωσι καὶ ... ἐρίσωσιν, with the subjunctive, is 'such men as wish ... and contend', and αὐτοὶ τοί γ’ ἀπάγουσι is the main verb, 'they themselves bring'. μνηστεύειν is 'to woo', and ἀφνειοῖο is the genitive of ἀφνειός 'rich', in -οιο. ἴφια μῆλα is 'stout flocks', and κούρης δαῖτα φίλοισι is 'for the girl a feast for her dear ones', φίλοισι being her own kin. ἀγλαὰ δῶρα is 'splendid gifts'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἀλλότριον βίοτον νήποινον ἔδουσιν.
sentences.l: but not another's living unpunished do they devour.”
sentences.i: but they do not devour another's living and pay nothing for it.”
sentences.n: ἀλλότριον is 'belonging to another', the word that was 'foreign' in ἀλλότριος φώς, line 219. βίοτον is 'living'. νήποινον is 'unpaid for' and so 'unpunished': the house English is 'unpunished' in the literal line and 'pay nothing for it' in the free line, which says what is meant here: the suitors take what they do not pay for. ἔδουσιν is the epic present of ἔδω 'eat, devour'. Penelope's speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δὲ πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
οὕνεκα τῶν μὲν δῶρα παρέλκετο, θέλγε δὲ θυμὸν
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι, νόος δέ οἱ ἄλλα μενοίνα.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and rejoiced much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
because from them gifts she drew out, and enchanted their heart
with gentle words, but his mind intended other things.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus rejoiced, because she was drawing gifts out of them and enchanting their hearts with gentle words, while his own mind intended other things.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is 'so she spoke', here of a woman, and πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the fixed 'much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus'. οὕνεκα is 'because'. παρέλκετο is the imperfect middle of παρέλκω 'draw aside, draw out for oneself', so she was drawing gifts out of the suitors; τῶν is 'from them'. θέλγε is the imperfect of θέλγω 'enchant', and θυμόν is 'heart'. μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι is 'gentle words'. οἱ in νόος δέ οἱ is the dative 'to him, his', and ἄλλα μενοίνα is 'was intending other things', μενοινάω being 'have in mind, intend': the last clause is Odysseus' own, set against the pleasure he takes in her trick.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος προσέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός,
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed Antinous, Eupeithes' son:
sentences.i: Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction. τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ is 'her then in turn', and προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι 'speak to'. Εὐπείθεος υἱός is 'son of Eupeithes', the genitive Εὐπείθεος in -εος. The text prints a comma after υἱός where the same formula elsewhere has a raised point; the unit ends here all the same, since the speech begins in the next.

sentences.t:
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρον Πηνελόπεια,
δῶρα μὲν ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν Ἀχαιῶν ἐνθάδ’ ἐνεῖκαι,
δέξασθ’.
sentences.l:
“Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope,
gifts, whichever of the Achaeans is willing to bring here,
accept them.
sentences.i: “Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, accept the gifts that any of the Achaeans is willing to bring here.
sentences.n: δῶρα μέν is 'as for gifts', and ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν is 'whoever is willing', with the subjunctive ἐθέλῃσιν in -σιν. ἐνεῖκαι is the aorist infinitive 'to bring' (Attic ἐνεγκεῖν), the same verb as ἔνεικε in lines 292-301. δέξασθ’ is most simply the aorist middle infinitive δέξασθαι, elided and used as an imperative ('receive!'), as γήμασθ’ was in Odysseus' words; Penelope is addressed alone, so a plural imperative δέξασθε is unlikely. The unit ends in the middle of line 287, at the full stop Murray prints there.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ καλὸν ἀνήνασθαι δόσιν ἐστίν·
sentences.l: for it is not fine to refuse a gift;
sentences.i: for it is not fine to refuse a gift;
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ καλόν is 'for it is not fine', καλός the word of fitting and handsome conduct. ἀνήνασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀναίνομαι 'refuse, reject', and δόσιν is 'gift, giving'. The word order puts ἐστίν last.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ οὔτ’ ἐπὶ ἔργα πάρος γ’ ἴμεν οὔτε πῃ ἄλλῃ,
πρίν γέ σε τῷ γήμασθαι Ἀχαιῶν ὅς τις ἄριστος.
sentences.l:
But we will not go, before then, to our own work, nor anywhere else,
until you marry him, whoever is best of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: And we will not go off to our own affairs, or anywhere else, until you marry whichever of the Achaeans is best.”
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δ’ is 'and we', the suitors as a body. ἴμεν is the first person plural of εἶμι, 'we go', with the sense of a future. πρίν γε σε τῷ γήμασθαι is 'until you marry him', γήμασθαι the aorist middle infinitive, of the woman who takes a husband; τῷ is 'him', the pronoun, and ὅς τις ἄριστος 'whoever is best'. The first line stands in an earlier part word for word.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀντίνοος, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος·
sentences.l: So spoke Antinous, and to them the word was pleasing.
sentences.i: So spoke Antinous, and his words pleased them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀντίνοος is 'so spoke Antinous', ἔφατο an imperfect middle of φημί. ἐπιήνδανε is 'was pleasing', the imperfect of ἐπιανδάνω, and τοῖσιν the pronoun 'to them', the suitors. μῦθος is 'a word, a speech'.

sentences.t: δῶρα δ’ ἄρ’ οἰσέμεναι πρόεσαν κήρυκα ἕκαστος.
sentences.l: and gifts to bring they sent a herald, each one.
sentences.i: and each one sent a herald off to fetch gifts.
sentences.n: δῶρα ... οἰσέμεναι is 'to bring gifts', οἰσέμεναι the epic future infinitive of φέρω, here expressing purpose. πρόεσαν is the aorist of προΐημι 'send forth', and ἕκαστος 'each one' stands last. The same verb for 'bring' in other forms, ἔνεικε, runs through the next lines.

sentences.t:
Ἀντινόῳ μὲν ἔνεικε μέγαν περικαλλέα πέπλον,
ποικίλον·
sentences.l:
For Antinous brought he a great, very fair robe,
intricate;
sentences.i: For Antinous the herald brought a great and very fair robe, intricately worked;
sentences.n: ἔνεικε is the aorist of φέρω 'bring', with no subject stated: it is the herald of line 291, and Ἀντινόῳ 'for Antinous' is a dative of the person for whom the gift comes. περικαλλής is 'very fair', and πέπλος is the robe, a woman's garment. ποικίλον 'intricate' says that the cloth was worked in a pattern. The raised point falls in the middle of line 293, and the pins of the robe follow.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἀρ’ ἔσαν περόναι δυοκαίδεκα πᾶσαι
χρύσειαι, κληῗσιν ἐϋγνάμπτοις ἀραρυῖαι.
sentences.l:
in it were pins, twelve, all
golden, in well-bent hooks fitted.
sentences.i: In it were twelve pins, all of gold, fitted with well-bent hooks.
sentences.n: ἐν ... ἔσαν is 'in it were', with ἔσαν the epic ἦσαν. περόναι are pins or brooches for fastening a robe; δυοκαίδεκα is 'twelve'. χρύσειαι is 'golden'. κληῗσιν ἐϋγνάμπτοις is a dative 'with well-bent hooks', κληΐς being a hook or clasp, and ἀραρυῖαι is a perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit, be fitted': the pins are fitted to the hooks.

sentences.t: ὅρμον δ’ Εὐρυμάχῳ πολυδαίδαλον αὐτίκ’ ἔνεικε.
sentences.l: A necklace for Eurymachus, much-wrought, at once he brought.
sentences.i: For Eurymachus his herald at once brought a richly wrought necklace.
sentences.n: ὅρμον is 'necklace', and πολυδαίδαλον 'much-wrought', a compound of πολύς and δαίδαλος 'skilfully made'. Εὐρυμάχῳ is the dative of the person the gift is for, as Ἀντινόῳ was. αὐτίκ’ is 'at once'; ἔνεικε is the verb of line 292.

sentences.t: χρύσεον, ἠλέκτροισιν ἐερμένον ἠέλιον ὥς.
sentences.l: golden, strung with amber, like the sun.
sentences.i: It was of gold, strung with beads of amber, bright as the sun.
sentences.n: The line has no verb of its own: χρύσεον 'golden' agrees with ὅρμον of line 295, and describes it; ἐερμένον is the perfect passive participle of εἴρω 'string, fasten in a row'. ἠλέκτροισιν is a dative plural of ἤλεκτρον, 'amber', although the word can also mean electrum, an alloy of gold and silver, which Homer's use does not decide. ἠέλιον ὥς is 'like the sun', with the epic ἠέλιος.

sentences.t:
ἕρματα δ’ Εὐρυδάμαντι δύω θεράποντες ἔνεικαν,
τρίγληνα μορόεντα·
sentences.l:
Earrings for Eurydamas two attendants brought,
three-eyed, mulberry-like;
sentences.i: Two attendants brought Eurydamas earrings with three drops, mulberry-like;
sentences.n: ἕρματα are earrings, and δύω is 'two'. θεράποντες is 'attendants', and Εὐρυδάμαντι the dative of the person for whom they brought them; here the gift is carried by two men, and not by one herald. The sense of both adjectives is not certain: τρίγληνα is understood as 'three-eyed', each earring having three small drops or beads, and μορόεντα as 'mulberry-like', clustered like mulberries. The raised point falls in the middle of line 298.

sentences.t: χάρις δ’ ἀπελάμπετο πολλή.
sentences.l: and grace shone from them, much.
sentences.i: and much grace shone from them.
sentences.n: χάρις is 'grace, charm', here the shine of fine craftsmanship. ἀπελάμπετο is the imperfect middle of ἀπολάμπω 'shine from, shine forth', and πολλή 'much' stands at the end.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα Πεισάνδροιο Πολυκτορίδαο ἄνακτος
ἴσθμιον ἤνεικεν θεράπων, περικαλλὲς ἄγαλμα.
sentences.l:
And from the lord Peisander, son of Polyctor,
a neck-band brought an attendant, a very fair ornament.
sentences.i: From the lord Peisander, son of Polyctor, an attendant brought a collar, a very fair ornament.
sentences.n: ἐκ ... ἤνεικεν is tmesis: the preverb stands apart from the verb of bringing, a different form (ἤνεικεν) from ἔνεικε above. Πεισάνδροιο Πολυκτορίδαο is 'of Peisander, son of Polyctor', both genitives in -οιο and -αο, and ἄνακτος is 'of the lord'. ἴσθμιον is something worn at the neck, ἰσθμός being 'neck, narrow passage', and ἄγαλμα is 'ornament, delight'. περικαλλές is 'very fair'.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δ’ ἄρ’ ἄλλος δῶρον Ἀχαιῶν καλὸν ἔνεικεν.
sentences.l: And another gift another of the Achaeans, a fine one, brought.
sentences.i: And each of the other Achaeans brought a different fine gift.
sentences.n: ἄλλο ... ἄλλος is a distributive pair: 'one a different gift, another a different one'. Ἀχαιῶν is a partitive genitive, 'of the Achaeans', the suitors. καλόν is 'fine', and ἔνεικεν the verb of bringing used since line 292.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀνέβαιν’ ὑπερώϊα δῖα γυναικῶν,
τῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ἅμ’ ἀμφίπολοι ἔφερον περικαλλέα δῶρα.
sentences.l:
She then went up to the upper rooms, heavenly-one of women,
and with her attendants carried the very fair gifts.
sentences.i: She went up to her upper rooms, heavenly among women, and her attendants carried the very fair gifts with her.
sentences.n: ἡ μέν is 'she', Penelope, and ἀνέβαιν’ is the imperfect of ἀναβαίνω 'go up'. ὑπερώϊα are the upper rooms, the women's quarters on the upper floor. δῖα γυναικῶν is 'heavenly among women'. τῇ δ’ ἅμ’ is 'and with her', and ἀμφίπολοι are 'attendants'; περικαλλέα is 'very fair'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ εἰς ὀρχηστύν τε καὶ ἱμερόεσσαν ἀοιδὴν
τρεψάμενοι τέρποντο, μένον δ’ ἐπὶ ἕσπερον ἐλθεῖν.
sentences.l:
And they to dancing and to lovely song
having turned, took their pleasure, and waited for evening to come.
sentences.i: The suitors turned to dancing and lovely song and took their pleasure in it, waiting for evening to come.
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is 'and they', the suitors, now that Penelope has gone up. ὀρχηστύς is 'dancing' and ἱμερόεσσαν is the feminine of ἱμερόεις 'lovely, full of longing'. τρεψάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of τρέπω, 'having turned themselves'. τέρποντο is the imperfect middle of τέρπω 'delight', and ἐπὶ ... ἐλθεῖν is tmesis for ἐπελθεῖν 'come on', with ἕσπερον 'evening' the accusative subject of the infinitive; μένον is the imperfect of μένω 'wait'.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ τερπομένοισι μέλας ἐπὶ ἕσπερος ἦλθεν.
sentences.l: And to them taking their pleasure dark evening came on.
sentences.i: As they took their pleasure, dark evening came on them.
sentences.n: τοῖσι δὲ τερπομένοισι is 'and to them, taking their pleasure', the dative of the persons the evening came upon, with the participle of τέρπω, which echoes τέρποντο in the line before. μέλας is 'dark'. ἐπὶ ... ἦλθεν is tmesis: ἐπῆλθεν 'came on', and ἕσπερος 'evening' is the same word as ἕσπερον above, here as the nominative subject.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα λαμπτῆρας τρεῖς ἵστασαν ἐν μεγάροισιν,
ὄφρα φαείνοιεν·
sentences.l:
At once braziers, three, they set up in the halls,
that they might give light;
sentences.i: At once they set up three braziers in the halls, to give light;
sentences.n: αὐτίκα is 'at once'. λαμπτῆρες are braziers, stands that held a burning fire for light. ἵστασαν is the imperfect of ἵστημι, 'set up', and no subject is named. ὄφρα φαείνοιεν is a purpose clause with the optative: φαείνω is 'give light, shine', and the braziers are its subject. The raised point falls in the middle of line 308.

sentences.t:
περὶ δὲ ξύλα κάγκανα θῆκαν,
αὖα πάλαι, περίκηλα, νέον κεκεασμένα χαλκῷ,
καὶ δαΐδας μετέμισγον·
sentences.i: and they laid dry logs around them, long since withered and well-dried, newly split with bronze, and mixed torches in among them;
sentences.n: περὶ ... θῆκαν is tmesis, 'put round them', the braziers. ξύλα κάγκανα is 'dry logs', and κάγκανα, αὖα and περίκηλα all mean 'dry'; the exact shades between them are not known to us. νέον κεκεασμένα χαλκῷ is 'newly split with bronze', the perfect passive participle of κεάζω 'split', and νέον the adverb 'newly'. δαΐδες are torches of resinous wood, and μετέμισγον is 'mixed in among', the imperfect of μετα-μίσγω. The raised point falls in the middle of line 310.

sentences.t:
ἀμοιβηδὶς δ’ ἀνέφαινον
δμῳαὶ Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος.
sentences.l:
and by turns they made them blaze,
the maidservants of Odysseus, enduring-minded.
sentences.i: and in turn the maids of steadfast Odysseus kept them blazing.
sentences.n: ἀμοιβηδίς is 'in turn, by turns', and ἀνέφαινον the imperfect of ἀναφαίνω 'make appear, cause to blaze up'. δμῳαί is 'maids', and ταλασίφρονος is the genitive of the epithet ταλασίφρων 'enduring-minded', τλῆναι 'endure' and φρήν 'mind'. Ὀδυσσῆος is a genitive in -ηος (Attic Ὀδυσσέως). The cut falls in the middle of line 311, after the full stop.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ τῇσιν
αὐτὸς διογενῆς μετέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l:
but he, to them
himself, Zeus-sprung, spoke among them, many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus himself, Zeus-born, of many wiles, spoke among them:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὁ τῇσιν is 'but he to them', τῇσιν an epic dative plural feminine of the pronoun, 'to the women'. αὐτός is 'himself, in person'. μετέφη is 'spoke among', and διογενής 'Zeus-born' and πολύμητις 'of many wiles' are standing epithets of Odysseus, rendered every time. A speech-introduction; the quotation marks open with the speech in the next unit.

sentences.t:
δμῳαὶ Ὀδυσσῆος, δὴν οἰχομένοιο ἄνακτος,
ἔρχεσθε πρὸς δώμαθ’, ἵν’ αἰδοίη βασίλεια·
sentences.l:
“Maidservants of Odysseus, the lord long gone,
go to the house, where the revered queen is;
sentences.i: “Maids of Odysseus, your lord so long gone, go to the house where the revered queen is;
sentences.n: δμῳαί is 'maids'. δὴν οἰχομένοιο ἄνακτος is 'the lord long gone', δήν 'long' and οἰχομένοιο the genitive of the participle of οἴχομαι 'be gone'; Odysseus speaks of himself in the third person, unrecognised. ἔρχεσθε is the imperative 'go', and δώμαθ’ the elided accusative plural of δῶμα, 'to the house'. ἵν’ is 'where', with the verb 'is' left out. αἰδοίη βασίλεια is 'the revered queen', αἰδοίη the feminine of αἰδοῖος 'worthy of respect'.

sentences.t:
τῇ δὲ παρ’ ἠλάκατα στροφαλίζετε, τέρπετε δ’ αὐτὴν
ἥμεναι ἐν μεγάρῳ, ἢ εἴρια πείκετε χερσίν·
sentences.l:
and by her the yarn spin, and delight her
sitting in the hall, or wool comb with your hands;
sentences.i: spin your yarn beside her, and please her as you sit in the hall, or comb wool with your hands;
sentences.n: τῇ δὲ παρ’ is 'and by her', παρά with the dative. ἠλάκατα are 'yarn', the wool drawn on the distaff, and στροφαλίζετε is 'twirl, spin'. τέρπετε is the imperative of τέρπω 'delight, please', and αὐτήν 'her'. ἥμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἧμαι 'sit' (Attic καθῆσθαι), and ἐν μεγάρῳ is 'in the hall'. εἴρια is 'wool', and πείκετε is the imperative of πείκω 'comb, card'.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τούτοισι φάος πάντεσσι παρέξω.
sentences.l: but I for these all will provide light.
sentences.i: I will provide light for all these men.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ here sets his task against the women's: they go to Penelope, he stays with the suitors. τούτοισι is the dative plural in -οισι, 'for these', the suitors, and πάντεσσι the epic dative plural in -εσσι, 'for all'. φάος is the epic form of φῶς 'light', and παρέξω the future of παρέχω 'provide'.

sentences.t:
ἤν περ γάρ κ’ ἐθέλωσιν ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ μίμνειν,
οὔ τί με νικήσουσι· πολυτλήμων δὲ μάλ’ εἰμί.
sentences.l:
For even if they should wish fair-throned Dawn to wait for,
not at all will they overcome me; and much-enduring very am I.”
sentences.i: For even if they wish to wait for fair-throned Dawn, they will not at all overcome me; I have very great endurance.”
sentences.n: ἤν περ γάρ κ’ is 'for even if', ἤν being ἐάν and κ’ κε. ἐθέλωσιν is the subjunctive, 'they wish', and μίμνειν is 'to wait for', with the accusative Ἠῶ 'Dawn'; ἐΰθρονον is 'fair-throned'. οὔ τί με νικήσουσι is 'they will not at all overcome me', the future of νικάω, here 'outlast'. πολυτλήμων is 'much-enduring', from πολύς and the root of τλῆναι; it is not the same word as πολύτλας but belongs to the same family, and Odysseus, speaking of himself, uses his own epithet's kind of word. μάλα is 'very'. Odysseus' speech ends here.
